en: The Path of Discrimination 1,
Great Chapter 1.3.
Discourse on Mindfulness of Breathing (Ānāpānassati)
1.3.1 The Chapter on Counting:
For one who develops concentration through mindfulness of breathing with its sixteen bases, more than two hundred kinds of knowledge arise:
eight kinds of knowledge regarding obstacles, eight kinds of knowledge regarding aids, eighteen kinds of knowledge regarding defilements, and thirteen...
There are knowledges of purification; thirty-two knowledges of one who dwells with mindfulness; twenty-four knowledges by way of concentration;
seventy-two knowledges by way of insight; eight knowledges of disenchantment; eight knowledges of conformity to disenchantment; eight knowledges of the subsiding of disenchantment;
and twenty-one knowledges in the bliss of liberation.
What are the eight knowledges of obstacles and the eight knowledges of aids?
Sensual desire is an obstacle to concentration; renunciation is an aid to concentration.
Ill will is an obstacle to concentration; non-ill will is an aid to concentration.
Lethargy and drowsiness are an obstacle to concentration; the perception of light is an aid to concentration.
Restlessness is an obstacle to concentration; non-distraction is an aid to concentration.
Doubt is an obstacle to concentration; the discernment of phenomena is an aid to concentration.
Ignorance is an obstacle to concentration; knowledge is an aid to concentration.
Discontent is an obstacle to concentration; gladness is an aid to concentration.
All unwholesome states are obstacles to concentration; all wholesome states are aids to concentration.
These are the eight kinds of knowledge regarding obstacles and the eight kinds of knowledge regarding aids.
This is the first section: the Enumeration.
1.3.2. The Exposition of the Sixteen Kinds of Knowledge.
In these sixteen ways, the appropriately directed mind and the thoroughly directed mind settle in unity and are purified from the hindrances.

What are those unities? Renunciation is a unity; non-ill will is a unity; perception of light is a unity; non-distraction is a unity; definition of phenomena is a unity; knowledge is a unity; gladness is a unity; and all wholesome states are also unities.
"Obstructions": what are those obstructions?
Sensual desire is an obstruction; ill will is an obstruction; sloth and torpor are an obstruction; restlessness and remorse are an obstruction;
doubt is an obstruction; ignorance is an obstruction; discontent is an obstruction; indeed, all unwholesome states are obstructions.
"Obstructions": in what sense are they obstructions?
They are obstructions in the sense of obstructing the way out.
What are those ways out?
Renunciation is the outlet for the noble ones;
by means of that renunciation, the noble ones go forth.
Sensual desire is the obstruction to the outlet.
Because one is shrouded by that sensual desire, one does not understand renunciation, which is the escape for the Noble Ones;
thus, sensual desire is an obstruction to escape.
Non-ill will is the escape for the Noble Ones.
And by means of that non-ill will, the noble ones go forth.
Ill will is an obstruction to going forth.
Because they are shrouded by that ill will, they do not understand non-ill will as the going forth of the noble ones. Thus it is said.
Ill will is an obstruction to the way out.
Perception of light is the way out for the noble ones;
and by means of that perception of light, the noble ones go forth.
Lethargy and drowsiness are an obstruction to the way out.
Because one is shrouded by that lethargy and drowsiness, one does not understand the perception of light—the way out for the noble ones;
thus, lethargy and drowsiness are an obstruction to the way out.
Non-distraction is the escape for the noble ones;
by means of that non-distraction, the noble ones escape.
Restlessness is the obstruction to escape.
Because one is shrouded by that restlessness, one does not understand non-distraction—the escape for the Noble Ones;
thus, restlessness is an obstruction to escape.
The discernment of phenomena is the escape for the Noble Ones.
And by means of that definition of phenomena, the Noble Ones go forth.
Doubt is an obstruction to going forth.
Because they are shrouded by that doubt, they do not understand the Noble Ones’ going forth, which is the definition of phenomena. Thus it is said.
Doubt is an obstruction to deliverance.
Knowledge is the deliverance of the Noble Ones;
by means of that knowledge, the Noble Ones are delivered.
Ignorance is an obstruction to the way out.
Because it is shrouded by that ignorance, the knowledge of the Noble Ones does not discern the way out;
thus, ignorance is an obstruction to the way out.
Joy is the escape for the noble ones;
by means of that joy, the noble ones escape.
Discontent is the obstruction to escape.
And because one is shrouded by that discontent, one does not understand joy as the escape for the noble ones;
thus, discontent is an obstruction to escape.
All wholesome states are the escape for the noble ones.
By means of those wholesome states, the noble ones go forth.
All unwholesome states are obstructions to going forth.
Because they are shrouded by those unwholesome states, the noble ones do not understand the wholesome states that constitute their going forth.
All unwholesome states are obstacles to deliverance.
The second section: The Exposition of the Sixteen Knowledges.
1.3.3. The Exposition of the Knowledge of Imperfections.

1.3.3.1. The First Sixfold Set Furthermore, for one whose mind has been purified of these hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and who is developing concentration through mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) based on the sixteen bases, eighteen defilements (*upakkilesa*) arise due to momentary conjunctions. What are they?
When one follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the inhalation, the mind becomes distracted internally; this is an obstacle to concentration.
For one who follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the out-breath, a mind that has wandered toward external distraction is an obstacle to concentration.
Longing for the in-breath, attachment, and the practice of craving are obstacles to concentration.
Longing for the out-breath, attachment, and the practice of craving are obstacles to concentration.
For one who is overwhelmed by the inhalation, the longing for the attainment of the exhalation is an obstacle to concentration.
For one who is overwhelmed by the exhalation, the longing for the attainment of the inhalation is an obstacle to concentration.
And the following after the inhalation—
Following after the out-breath is internal distraction;
doubt is external distraction and longing.
The release upon obtaining the out-breath for one who was oppressed by the in-breath; the release upon obtaining the in-breath for one who was oppressed by the out-breath.
Delusion upon the attainment of consolation—
these six are the defilements of concentration on mindfulness of breathing.
For one who is thus distracted and whose mind is not liberated,
not understanding liberation—
These are dependent on the conviction of others.
1.3.3.2. The Second Hexad:
When one adverts to the sign, the mind wavers during inhalation.
It is an obstacle to concentration.
When one adverts to the inhalation, the mind wavers toward the sign—
this is an obstacle to concentration.
When one adverts to the sign, the mind wavers regarding the out-breath;
this is an obstacle to concentration.
When one adverts to the out-breath, the mind wavers regarding the sign; [this too is an obstacle to concentration].
It is an obstacle to concentration.
When one directs attention to the inhalation, the mind wavers toward the exhalation—
this is an obstacle to concentration.
When one adverts to the out-breath, the mind wavers regarding the in-breath;
this is an obstacle to concentration.
When one adverts to the sign...
The mind becomes distracted during the inhalation;
for one who adverts to the inhalation,
the consciousness wavers from the sign.
For one who adverts to the sign,
the mind becomes distracted by the out-breath;
for one who adverts to the out-breath—
The mind wavers toward the sign.
When one adverts to the inhalation,
the mind is distracted by the exhalation.
For one who is attending to the out-breath,
the mind wavers during the in-breath.
These are the six defilements.
Of the concentration of mindfulness on breathing,
by which, when distracted,
the mind is not liberated.
Not understanding liberation, they become dependent on others for faith.
1.3.3.3. The Third Sixfold Set.
A mind that pursues the past has fallen into distraction—
it is an obstacle to concentration.
A mind that anticipates the future is agitated— it is an obstacle to concentration.
Lethargy is an obstacle to concentration.
A mind that is sluggish and fallen into indolence is an obstacle to concentration.
A mind that is over-exerted and beset by restlessness is an obstacle to concentration.
A mind that is drawn inward and beset by lust—
The mind that has been drawn away and fallen into ill will is an obstacle to concentration.
The mind that pursues the past,
the longing for the future, the sluggish,
the over-exerted, and the over-inclined—
A mind that is withdrawn does not become concentrated.
These six are the defilements of concentration through mindfulness of breathing.
"One whose intention is defiled by these does not understand higher consciousness.

For one who follows the beginning, middle, and end of the breath with mindfulness, because the mind has become distracted internally, both the body and the mind become agitated, shaken, and trembling.

For one who follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the out-breath, the body and the mind become agitated, disturbed, and restless due to a mind that has strayed into external distraction.
Due to the longing for, the attachment to, and the conduct of craving for the in-breath, the body and the mind become agitated, disturbed, and restless.
Due to the longing for, the attachment to, and the conduct of craving for the out-breath, the body and the mind become agitated, disturbed, and restless.
When one who is overwhelmed by the in-breath fails to obtain the out-breath, because of that state of fainting, both body and mind become agitated, disturbed, and tremulous.
When one who is overwhelmed by the out-breath fails to obtain the in-breath, because of that state of fainting, both body and mind become agitated, disturbed, and tremulous.
When one adverts to the sign, because the mind is shaken during the in-breath, both body and mind become agitated, disturbed, and tremulous.
When one adverts to the inhalation, because the mind wavers toward the sign, both body and mind become agitated, restless, and trembling.
When one adverts to the sign, because the mind wavers toward the exhalation, both body and mind become agitated, restless, and trembling.
When one adverts to the exhalation, because the mind wavers toward the sign, both body and mind become agitated, restless, and trembling.
When one adverts to the out-breath while the mind is distracted by the in-breath, both body and mind become excited, agitated, and tremulous.
When one adverts to the in-breath while the mind is distracted by the out-breath, both body and mind become excited, agitated, and tremulous.
Through a mind that pursues the past and is beset by distraction, both body and mind become excited, agitated, and tremulous.
With a mind that anticipates the future and is wavering, both body and mind become agitated, disturbed, and tremulous.
With a sluggish mind fallen into indolence, both body and mind become agitated, disturbed, and tremulous.
With a mind over-exerted and fallen into restlessness, both body and mind become agitated, disturbed, and tremulous.
With a mind that has bent toward passion, both body and mind become agitated, wavering, and trembling.
With a mind that has bent toward ill will, both body and mind become agitated, wavering, and trembling.
For one who possesses mindfulness of breathing...
Though perfected, it is not developed;
the body wavers,
and the mind also wavers.
The body is agitated,
and the mind is also agitated—
this is for one who lacks mindfulness of breathing.
Fully perfected and well-developed;
the body is unshakable,
and the mind is also unshakable.
"The body becomes motionless and the mind also becomes motionless. Furthermore,

for one whose mind has been purified of these hindrances and who is developing the concentration of mindfulness of breathing with its sixteen bases, these eighteen imperfections arise through momentary conjunction.
The third section: The Description of Knowledge of Imperfections.
1.3.4. The Description of Knowledge of Purification.
What are the thirteen kinds of knowledge of purification?
A mind that pursues the past has fallen into distraction;
having avoided that, one concentrates on a single point—
in this way, too, the mind does not fall into distraction.
When the mind is shaken by longing for the future,
one avoids that and instead resolves right there;
in this way, the mind does not fall into distraction.
A mind that is sluggish has fallen into indolence;
by uplifting it, one abandons indolence—
in this way too, the mind does not fall into distraction.
A mind that is over-exerted is beset by restlessness;
by restraining it, one abandons restlessness—
in this way, too, the mind does not fall into distraction.
A mind that is bent and fallen under the influence of lust:
by being fully aware, one abandons that lust;
in this way, too, the mind does not fall into distraction.
When the mind has fallen into ill will,
one becomes fully aware and abandons that ill will;
in this way, too, the mind does not fall into distraction.
By these six bases, the mind becomes purified, cleansed, and attained to unity.
What are those unities?
The unity established by giving and relinquishing; the unity established by the sign of serenity; the unity established by the characteristic of vanishing; the unity established by cessation.

The singleness of the mind established upon the relinquishing of gifts belongs to those intent on generosity; the singleness of the mind established upon the sign of serenity belongs to those devoted to higher consciousness; the singleness of the mind established upon the characteristic of vanishing belongs to those practicing insight;

and the singleness of the mind established upon cessation belongs to noble persons. By these four stages, the mind that has attained singleness enters into purification of the way, is nourished by equanimity, and is gladdened by knowledge.
What is the beginning of the first jhāna? What is its middle? What is its end?
For the first jhāna, purification of the way is the beginning, the intensification of equanimity is the middle, and encouragement is the end.
Purification of the way is the beginning of the first jhāna.
How many characteristics does the beginning have?
Specifically, there are three characteristics:
the mind is purified from whatever obstacle it has; because it is purified, the mind enters upon the middle sign of serenity; and because it has entered upon it, the mind leaps into that state.

And that which is the purification of the mind from obstacles, and that which is the mind’s entering upon the middle sign of serenity through being purified, and that which is the mind’s leaping into that state through having entered upon it.
The purification of the way is the beginning of the first jhāna.
These are the three characteristics of a beginning.
Therefore it is said:
“The first jhāna is both excellent in the beginning and endowed with its characteristics.
What is the intensification of equanimity for the first jhāna?
How many characteristics does the middle [jhāna] have?
There are three characteristics of equanimity:
he looks on with equanimity at the purified mind; he looks on with equanimity at that which has entered into calm; he looks on with equanimity at the establishment of unity.

That which he looks on with equanimity at as the purified mind, that which he looks on with equanimity at as having entered into calm, and that which he looks on with equanimity at as the establishment of unity—[these are the three characteristics].
The intensification of equanimity belongs to the middle of the first jhāna.
These are its three characteristics.
Therefore it is said:
“The first jhāna is beautiful in the middle and endowed with the [proper] characteristics.
This is the conclusion of the praise of the first jhāna.
How many characteristics does the conclusion have?
There are four characteristics of the conclusion.

Therein, encouragement is in the sense of non-transgression of the states that have arisen; encouragement is in the sense of the single flavor of the faculties; encouragement is in the sense of the exertion of the appropriate energy; encouragement is in the sense of repetition.
Encouragement regarding the first jhāna is the conclusion.
These are the four characteristics of the conclusion.
Therefore it is said:
“The first jhāna is beautiful in its conclusion and endowed with characteristics.”
Thus, the mind that has reached the three stages is good in three ways and endowed with ten characteristics;
it is endowed with applied thought and sustained thought, and it is endowed with rapture,
pleasure, the resolution of the mind, faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
What is the beginning of the second jhāna? What is its middle? What is its end?
The purification of the way is the beginning of the second jhāna; the intensification of equanimity is the middle; the encouragement is the end.
… Thus the mind, having reached the three stages, being good in three ways and endowed with ten characteristics, is indeed endowed with rapture.
It becomes endowed with happiness, endowed with resolve of mind, endowed with faith, endowed with energy, endowed with mindfulness, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom.
What is the beginning of the third jhāna? What is its middle? What is its end? …pe…
Thus, the mind that has reached the three stages is excellent in three ways and endowed with ten characteristics;
it is endowed with happiness and endowed with the mind’s resolution, and it is endowed with faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
What is the beginning of the fourth jhāna? What is its middle? What is its end?

… Thus, the mind that has reached the three stages is excellent in three ways, endowed with ten characteristics, and is indeed endowed with equanimity, as well as endowed with the mind’s resolution, endowed with faith, endowed with energy, and endowed with mindfulness.
One who is perfected in concentration and perfected in wisdom.
[The same applies to] the attainment of the base of infinite space …pe… the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness …
What is the beginning, what is the middle, and what is the end of the attainment of the base of nothingness … the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?

… Thus the mind, having proceeded through the three stages, being excellent in its three aspects and endowed with ten characteristics, becomes both endowed with equanimity and endowed with the resolution of the mind … [and so forth].
And endowed with wisdom.
What is the beginning, what is the middle, and what is the end of the contemplation of impermanence? ...
Thus, the mind that has proceeded through the three stages is excellent in its three aspects, endowed with the ten characteristics, and possessed of applied thought.

It becomes endowed with investigation, endowed with rapture, endowed with pleasure, endowed with mental resolve, endowed with faith, endowed with energy, endowed with mindfulness, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom.
[The same applies to] the contemplation of suffering... [and so on].
through the contemplation of non-self … through the contemplation of disenchantment … through the contemplation of dispassion …
... by means of the contemplation of cessation ...
by means of the contemplation of relinquishment ...
by means of the contemplation of destruction ...
contemplation of vanishing … contemplation of change … contemplation of the signless …
... by means of the contemplation of the wishless ...
by means of the contemplation of emptiness ...
by means of higher wisdom and insight into phenomena ...
for the sake of knowing and seeing things as they truly are … for the contemplation of danger … for the contemplation of reflective discernment …
...of the contemplation of turning away ...
of the path of stream-entry ... [and so on] ...
of the path of once-returning ...
What is the beginning, what is the middle, and what is the end of the path of non-returning … of the path of arahantship? For the path of arahantship,
purification of the way is the beginning, the intensification of equanimity is the middle, and encouragement is the end.
The purification of the way is the beginning of the path of arahantship.
How many characteristics does the beginning have?
The beginning has three characteristics.

The mind is purified from whatever constitutes an obstacle to it; because of that purification, the mind enters upon the middle sign of serenity; and because it has entered upon it, the mind leaps forward into it.

That the mind is purified from obstacles, that through purification the mind enters upon the middle sign of serenity, and that having entered upon it the mind leaps forward into it—this is the beginning of the purification of the way to the path of arahantship.
Taken individually, these are the three characteristics.
Therefore it is said:
“The path to arahantship is beautiful in the beginning and endowed with characteristics.”
The cultivation of equanimity belongs to the middle [part] of the path of arahantship.
How many characteristics does the middle have?
The middle has three characteristics.
He looks on with equanimity at the purified mind; he looks on with equanimity at that which has entered into calm; he looks on with equanimity at the establishment of unity.

Because he looks on with equanimity at the purified mind, looks on with equanimity at that which has entered into calm, and looks on with equanimity at the establishment of unity, therefore it is said:
“The path to arahantship is beautiful in the middle and endowed with the [proper] characteristics.
The praise of the path to arahantship is the conclusion.
How many characteristics does the conclusion have?
There are four characteristics of the conclusion.

Among these, encouragement is in the sense of not overstepping the states that have arisen; encouragement is in the sense of the single function of the faculties; encouragement is in the sense of driving forward the energy appropriate thereto; encouragement is in the sense of repetition.
Encouragement pertaining to the path of arahantship is the conclusion.
These are the four characteristics of the conclusion.
Therefore it is said:
"The path to arahantship is beautiful in its conclusion and endowed with characteristics."
Thus, the mind that has reached the three stages is good in three ways and endowed with ten characteristics;
it is endowed with applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), endowed with rapture (*pīti*) and happiness (*sukha*),
and endowed with the mind’s resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*), faith (*saddhā*), energy (*vīriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*).
The sign is the in-breath and out-breath,
which are not the object of a single moment of consciousness;
and for one who does not know these three things, [there is no attainment].
No cultivation is apprehended;
the sign consists of inhalation and exhalation,
which are not the object of a single moment of consciousness.
"And for one who knows these three things,
development is found.
How is it that these three things do not become objects for a single moment of consciousness, yet these three things are not unknown?
Do they arise, and does the mind not fall into distraction, such that exertion is evident, the application is accomplished,
and a distinction is attained?
It is just as if a tree were placed on a level stretch of ground.
A man might cut that tree with a saw.
By means of the saw-teeth as they touch the tree, the man’s mindfulness becomes established;
he does not attend to the saw-teeth as they come or go.
The saw-teeth are neither perceived as coming nor going; yet exertion is evident and the application achieves its purpose.
Just as a tree trunk placed on level ground [remains steady], such is the sign of the anchoring.
Just as with the teeth of a saw, so it is with the in-breaths and out-breaths.

Just as a person’s mindfulness is established by means of the teeth of a saw touching a tree, yet he does not attend to the teeth of the saw as they come or go, nor are the teeth of the saw coming or going unknown to him; [so too with the breaths].
He is seen making an effort and accomplishing his application.
In the same way, a bhikkhu sits having established mindfulness at the tip of the nose or on the upper lip;
he does not direct his mind to the incoming or outgoing breaths, nor are the incoming or outgoing breaths unknown to him as they come and go.
There is exertion, and striving is evident, and he accomplishes the application;
he attains distinction and exerts himself.
What is that exertion?
For one who has aroused energy, both body and mind become wieldy—
this is the striving.
What is the application?
The defilements of one who has aroused energy are abandoned, and discursive thoughts are stilled—
this is the application.
What is the distinction?
In one who has aroused energy, the fetters are abandoned and the underlying tendencies are brought to an end.
This is the distinction.
Thus, these three states do not become objects for a single moment of consciousness, yet these three states are not unknown.
And his mind does not wander, his striving becomes evident, he accomplishes the application, and he attains distinction.
For one whose mindfulness of breathing is fulfilled and well-developed:
Gradually cultivated,
just as taught by the Buddha,
he illuminates this world.
"Like the moon released from clouds":
"āna" is inhalation, not exhalation;
"apāna" is exhalation, not inhalation.

Mindfulness is the establishment [of awareness] by way of inhalation; mindfulness is the establishment [of awareness] by way of exhalation. It is established for whoever inhales; it is established for whoever exhales.
It is "complete" in the sense of encompassing, in the sense of surrounding, and in the sense of being fulfilled.
"Well-developed" refers to the four modes of development:

development in the sense of non-excess of the states arisen therein; development in the sense of single function (taste) of the faculties; development in the sense of the driving of energy directed toward that end; and development in the sense of repetition.
These four modes of development have been practiced, established as a foundation, consolidated, accumulated, and well undertaken by him.
"Made into a vehicle" means that wherever one desires, there one has attained mastery, attained strength, and attained fearlessness.
For me, those states are dependent upon advertence, dependent upon desire, dependent upon attention, and dependent upon the arising of consciousness.
Therefore it is said:
“Having made it a vehicle”:
having made it a foundation means that in whatever object the mind is well-established, in that very object mindfulness is well-settled;
or rather, in whatever object mindfulness is well-settled, in that very object the mind is well-established.
Therefore it is said:
"made a basis.
"Established" means that upon whatever object the mind is directed, mindfulness follows along with it.
Or rather, by whatever [object] mindfulness follows, toward that very object the mind is directed.
Therefore it is called "established."
"Fully cultivated" means fully cultivated in the sense of encompassing, fully cultivated in the sense of surrounding, and fully cultivated in the sense of fulfilling.
One who encompasses with mindfulness conquers evil, unwholesome states.
Therefore it is said:
“Cultivated” means well-undertaken. There are four ways it is well-undertaken:
it is well-undertaken in the sense of not overstepping the states arisen therein; it is well-undertaken in the sense of the faculties having a single function (ekarasa).

It is well-undertaken in the sense of being carried by energy that has approached that [object]; it is well-undertaken because of the thorough eradication of the defilements that are its opposites. Regarding "well" (*su*):
there is "even" (*sama*) and there is "very even" (*susama*).
What is the even?
Those things born therein that are blameless, wholesome, and conducive to enlightenment—
this is the even.
What is the most perfectly peaceful?
That which is the object of those various states— the cessation, Nibbāna—
this is the most perfectly peaceful.
Thus this and that are known, seen, understood, realized, and touched by means of wisdom—as being even and perfectly even.
Energy is aroused and not slackened; mindfulness is established and not confused; the body is tranquil and not agitated; the mind is concentrated and one-pointed.
Therefore, it is said:
“Thoroughly undertaken”:
it means accumulated in successive order. By way of long inhalation, each preceding [moment] is accumulated and each succeeding one is further accumulated.
By way of long exhalation, each preceding [moment] is accumulated and each succeeding one is further accumulated.
By means of short inhalations, each preceding one is cultivated and each succeeding one is further cultivated.
By means of short exhalations, each preceding one is cultivated and each succeeding one is further cultivated...
[and so on] ...by means of inhalations while contemplating relinquishment, each preceding one is cultivated and each succeeding one is further cultivated.
By way of out-breaths accompanied by the contemplation of relinquishment, each preceding [moment] is cultivated and each succeeding one is further cultivated.
Thus, all sixteen bases of mindfulness of breathing are both mutually cultivated and further cultivated.
Therefore, it is said:
“Gradually accumulated. As for “how”:
there are ten meanings of “how”:
the meaning of self-taming is the meaning of “how”; the meaning of self-pacification is the meaning of “how”; the meaning of self-extinguishing is the meaning of “how.”

The meaning of direct knowledge is the meaning as it truly is; the meaning of full understanding is the meaning as it truly is; the meaning of abandoning is the meaning as it truly is; the meaning of development is the meaning as it truly is;

the meaning of realization is the meaning as it truly is; the meaning of the convergence of the truths is the meaning as it truly is; the meaning of establishing in cessation is the meaning as it truly is.

"Buddha" refers to that Blessed One who is self-become, without a teacher, who by himself fully awakened to the truths regarding phenomena unheard before, and therein attained omniscience and mastery over the powers.
In what sense is he "Buddha"?
He is called "Buddha" because he has awakened to the truths.
He is "Buddha" because he awakens people;
he is "Buddha" because of his omniscience.
He is called Buddha because of his all-seeing vision;
he is called Buddha because of his state of not being led by others;
he is called Buddha because of his penetrating insight.
He is called "Buddha" because he has destroyed the taints;
he is called "Buddha" because he is unsullied; he is one who is entirely free from passion.
Buddho.
He is called "Buddho" because he has completely abandoned hatred.
One who is entirely free from delusion is a Buddha; one who is entirely free from defilement is a Buddha.
Buddho.
He has gone the path that goes alone—
thus he is "Buddho."
He is called “Buddha” because he has awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment alone,
and because he has attained wisdom through the destruction of non-wisdom.
"Buddha.
This name "Buddha" was not given by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brother,
nor by his sister, nor by friends and colleagues, nor by kinsmen and blood relations, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by deities.
This is the designation, realized at the root of the Bodhi tree by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, simultaneously with the acquisition of omniscient knowledge, namely:

"Buddha. As for "taught": it has the sense of self-taming, it has that sense according to how it was taught by the Buddha; it has the sense of self-calming, it has that sense according to how it was taught by the Buddha; it has the sense of self-extinction, it has that sense according to how it was taught by the Buddha... [and so on].
The meaning of "establishing in cessation" is the meaning of "suchness," just as it was taught by the Buddha.
"He" refers to one who is either a householder or one who has gone forth.

"The world" refers to the world of aggregates, the world of elements, the world of sense bases, the world of misfortune and existence, the world of the origin of misfortune, the world of prosperity and existence, and the world of the origin of prosperity.
One world:
all beings subsist on nutriment … [and so on] … eighteen worlds.
The eighteen elements.
He illuminates because he has perfectly awakened to the meaning of "taming oneself" as it truly is.
He illumines, speaks of, and illuminates this world.
Because he has fully awakened to the reality of the goal of self-composure;
therefore, he illuminates, speaks of, and radiates light throughout this world.
Because he has fully awakened to the reality of the goal of the complete extinguishing of the self.
Thus he illuminates, speaks of, and radiantly illumines this world...
[as before] ...because he has fully awakened to the meaning of reality as it is, establishing others in cessation.
Thus he illuminates, speaks of, and radiantly illumines this world.
"Just as the moon when freed from clouds": as the clouds are, so are the defilements;
as the moon is, so is noble knowledge;
as the divine son Candima is, so is the bhikkhu.
Just as the moon, when released from clouds, released from mist, released from smoke and dust, and completely freed from the grasp of Rāhu,
shines, glows, and radiates, even so the bhikkhu, completely freed from all defilements, shines, glows, and radiates. Therefore it is said:
“Like the moon freed from clouds.
These are the thirteen knowledges of purification.
This is the fourth chapter: The Description of the Knowledge of Purification.
The Recitation Section.
1.3.5. Exposition of the Knowledge of One Who Acts with Mindfulness.
What are the thirty-two kinds of knowledge of one who acts with mindfulness?

Here, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him, he breathes in mindfully and breathes out mindfully.
Breathing in long, he understands: "I am breathing in long."
Breathing in long, he knows, "I am breathing in long"; breathing out long, he knows, "I am breathing out long.
Breathing in short, he knows, "I am breathing in short";
breathing out short, he knows, "I am breathing out short."
“He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body.
He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.
He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation.’”
“He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.
He trains thus: ‘Experiencing rapture… experiencing pleasure…’”
Experiencing the mental formations … pacifying the mental formations … experiencing the mind …
Gladdening the mind… concentrating the mind… liberating the mind…
Contemplating impermanence … contemplating dispassion … contemplating cessation …
“He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment.
He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.
Herein: in this view, in this inclination, in this preference, in this adoption, in this Dhamma.”
In this Vinaya, in this Dhamma-Vinaya, in this teaching, in this holy life, in this instruction of the Teacher.
Therefore, it is said: "here."
"A bhikkhu" means one who is either a virtuous worldling, a trainee, or an arahant whose nature is unshakable.
"Forest" means that having gone out beyond the threshold post, all this is forest.
"At the foot of a tree" means wherever a seat for a bhikkhu has been prepared—whether it be a couch, a bench, or a mattress.
Whether it be a wooden platform, a piece of hide, a grass mat, a leaf mat, or a straw mat—
therein a bhikkhu walks back and forth, stands, sits, or lies down.
"Empty" means it is not crowded by anyone, whether householders or those gone forth.
"A house" means a monastery, a gabled hall, a palace, a pavilion, or a cave.
"Having sat down cross-legged" means he is seated with his legs folded crosswise.
"Holding the body erect" means the body is held straight and well-poised.
"Having established mindfulness at the mouth": *pari* has the sense of encompassing;
*mukha* has the sense of an outlet;
*sati* has the sense of establishing.
Therefore it is said:
"having established mindfulness facing the front.
"Mindfully he breathes in, mindfully he breathes out" means that he acts with mindfulness by way of thirty-two modes.
For one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction through long inhalation, mindfulness is established.
Through that mindfulness and that knowledge, one acts with mindfulness.
For one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction through long exhalation, mindfulness is established.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one acts with mindfulness.
For one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction through short inhalation, mindfulness is established.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one acts with mindfulness.
For one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction by means of short out-breaths, mindfulness is established.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, he acts with mindfulness … [and so on] … he is a contemplator of relinquishment by means of in-breaths …
When one understands one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of out-breath while contemplating relinquishment, mindfulness is established.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one acts with mindfulness.
1.3.5.1. Exposition of the First Tetrad.
How does one, breathing in long, know "I am breathing in long," and breathing out long, know "I am breathing out long"?

One breathes in a long inhalation reckoned as a duration; one breathes out a long exhalation reckoned as a duration; one both breathes in and breathes out a long inhalation and exhalation reckoned as a duration.
As one breathes in and breathes out a long inhalation and exhalation reckoned as a duration, zeal arises.
By means of desire, he breathes in a long inhalation even more subtle than that, reckoned as a duration;
by means of desire, he breathes out a long exhalation even more subtle than that, reckoned as a duration;
by means of desire, he breathes in and breathes out a long inhalation and exhalation even more subtle than that, reckoned as a duration.
By means of zeal, as he breathes in and breathes out a longer inhalation and exhalation—more subtle than that which was reckoned as a duration—joy arises.
By means of joy, he breathes in a longer inhalation more subtle than that, reckoned as a duration;
by means of joy, he breathes out a longer exhalation more subtle than that, reckoned as a duration; by means of joy, [he breathes] even more subtly than that...
One breathes in and breathes out long inhalations and exhalations reckoned as a duration.

Through the influence of gladness, one breathes in and breathes out even longer inhalations and exhalations than that, reckoned as a duration; and while breathing in and breathing out these long inhalations and exhalations, the mind turns away from them and equanimity becomes established.
In these nine ways, the long inhalations and exhalations are the body.
Establishment is mindfulness.
Contemplation is knowledge.
The body is the establishment, but not the mindfulness;
Mindfulness is both the establishment [of mindfulness] and mindfulness itself.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one contemplates that body.
Therefore it is said:
“Development of the foundation of mindfulness through contemplation of the body as a body.
How does one contemplate that body?
One contemplates it as impermanent, not as permanent.
He contemplates it as suffering, not as pleasure;
he contemplates it as non-self, not as self;
he becomes disenchanted with it, not delighted by it.
One becomes dispassionate, not impassioned;
one causes cessation, not origination;
one relinquishes, one does not grasp.
Contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence.
Contemplating as suffering, one abandons the perception of pleasure.
Contemplating as non-self, one abandons the perception of self.
By becoming disenchanted, one abandons delight.
By becoming dispassionate, one abandons lust.
By bringing about cessation, one abandons origination.
Relinquishing, one abandons grasping.
Thus one contemplates that body.
As for "development," there are four kinds of development:

In this context, "development" (bhāvanā) is in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein; development is in the sense of the single flavor of the faculties; development is in the sense of the exertion of the appropriate energy; development is in the sense of repeated practice.
For one who understands the unification and non-distraction of the mind by means of long inhalation and exhalation, feelings arise known, they persist known, and they subside known.
Perceptions arise known, they persist known, and they subside known.
Thoughts arise known, they persist known, and they pass away known.
How do feelings arise known, persist known, and pass away known?
How is the arising of feeling known?
"With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling"—thus the arising of feeling is known in the sense of the arising of conditions.
"With the arising of craving, there is the arising of feeling"... [and so on].

"From the arising of kamma comes the arising of feeling," and "from the arising of contact comes the arising of feeling"— thus, through the sense of the arising of conditions, the arising of feeling is understood. Furthermore,
for one who sees the characteristic of generation, the arising of feeling is understood.
In this way, the arising of feeling is known.
How is the manifestation of feeling known?
For one who attends to it as impermanent, its manifestation as exhaustion is known.
When one attends to it as suffering, the manifestation as terror becomes known.
When one attends to it as non-self, the manifestation as emptiness becomes known.
In this way, the manifestation regarding feeling becomes known.
How is the subsiding of feeling known?
"With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of feeling"— thus,
in the sense of the cessation of conditions, the subsiding of feeling is known.
"With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of feeling" ...
"with the cessation of karma, there is the cessation of feeling" ...
"with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling"—thus, through the sense of the cessation of conditions, the subsiding of feeling is understood.
Even for one who sees the characteristic of change, the subsiding of feeling is known.
In this way, the subsiding of feeling is known. Thus, feelings arise known, they persist known, and they pass away known.
How are perceptions known as they arise, known as they persist, and known as they pass away?
How is the arising of perception known?
"With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of perception"—thus it is known.
The arising of perception is known in the sense of the origination of conditions.
"With the origination of craving, there is the origination of perception" ... [and so on] ...
"with the origination of kamma, there is the origination of perception" ... [and so on].
"With the arising of contact, there is the arising of perception"— thus,
the arising of perception is known in the sense of the arising of conditions.
For one who sees the characteristic of generation, the arising of perception is also known.
In this way, the arising of perception is known.
How is the manifestation of perception known?
For one who attends to it as impermanent, its manifestation as exhaustion is known.
When one attends to [the body] as suffering, the manifestation as terror becomes known.
When one attends to it as non-self, the manifestation as emptiness becomes known.
In this way, the manifestation of perception becomes known.
How is the passing away of perception known?
"With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of perception"—
thus, by way of the cessation of conditions, the passing away of perception is known.
With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of perception … with the cessation of karma,
there is the cessation of perception … with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of perception.
The subsiding of perception is known in the sense of the cessation of conditions;
the subsiding of perception is also known by one who sees the characteristic of change.
Thus the subsiding of perception is known.
Thus perceptions arise known, they persist known, and they pass away known.
How do thoughts arise known, persist known, and pass away known?
How is the arising of thoughts known?
"With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of applied thought"—thus the arising of applied thoughts is known in the sense of the arising of conditions.
"With the arising of craving, there is the arising of applied thoughts"... [and so on].
“With the arising of kamma, there is the arising of applied thought” … “with the arising of perception, there is the arising of applied thought”—
thus the arising of applied thoughts is known in the sense of the arising of conditions.
Even for one who perceives the characteristic of manifestation, the arising of thoughts is known.
In this way, the arising of thoughts is known.
How is the presence of thoughts known?
When one attends to [phenomena] as impermanent, the manifestation of exhaustion becomes known.
When one attends to them as suffering, the manifestation of terror becomes known.
When one attends to them as non-self, the manifestation of emptiness becomes known.
In this way, the appearance of thoughts is known.
How is the disappearance of thoughts known?
"With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of thoughts"—thus it is known.
The subsiding of applied thoughts is known in the sense of the cessation of conditions:
"With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of applied thoughts" ... [and so on] ...
"With the cessation of karma, there is the cessation of applied thoughts" ... [and so on].
"With the cessation of perception comes the cessation of applied thought"— thus, in the sense of the cessation of conditions, the subsiding of applied thoughts is known.
For one who sees the characteristic of change as well, the subsiding of applied thoughts is known.
In this way, the subsiding of thoughts is known.
In this way, thoughts are known as they arise, known as they persist, and known as they pass away.
Understanding one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of long inhalation and exhalation, he coordinates the faculties, understands their range, and penetrates their capacity …pe…
He synthesizes the path, he synthesizes the phenomena, he understands the domain, and he penetrates the capacity.
As for "he synthesizes the faculties," how does he synthesize the faculties?
He synthesizes the faculty of faith in the sense of resolution; he synthesizes the faculty of energy in the sense of exertion.
In the sense of establishing, it coordinates the faculty of mindfulness; in the sense of non-distraction, it coordinates the faculty of concentration;
in the sense of seeing, it coordinates the faculty of wisdom.
This person coordinates these faculties upon this object.
Therefore it is said:
“He brings the faculties into harmony.
And he understands the domain: that which is its object is its domain.
That which is its range is its object. One who understands is a person;
the understanding is wisdom.
Equanimity is the evenness of the appearance of the object; equanimity is the non-distraction of the mind; equanimity is the mental determination; equanimity is the purification of the mind.
"The meaning" refers to the meaning of blamelessness, the meaning of freedom from defilement, the meaning of purification, and the ultimate meaning.

"He penetrates" means he penetrates the meaning of the appearance of the object, he penetrates the meaning of the non-distraction of the mind, he penetrates the meaning of the mental determination, and he penetrates the meaning of the purification of the mind.
Therefore it is said:
"And he penetrates what is possible.
How does he bring the powers together? How does he assemble the powers?
One combines the power of faith in the sense of being unshakable by lack of faith; one combines the power of energy in the sense of being unshakable by laziness;
one combines the power of mindfulness in the sense of being unshakable by negligence; one combines the power of concentration in the sense of being unshakable by restlessness;
and one combines the power of wisdom in the sense of being unshakable by ignorance.
This person combines these powers upon this object.
Therefore it is said:
"He combines the powers."
"And he understands the range of experience" ... [as before] ...
therefore it is said:
"and he penetrates what is possible."
"He brings the factors of enlightenment together": how does he bring the factors of enlightenment together?
He brings the mindfulness factor of enlightenment together in the sense of establishing; he brings the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment together in the sense of investigating;
he brings the energy factor of enlightenment together in the sense of exerting; he brings the rapture factor of enlightenment together in the sense of pervading.

He brings them together: he brings together the factor of enlightenment of tranquility in the sense of calming; he brings together the factor of enlightenment of concentration in the sense of non-distraction;
he brings together the factor of enlightenment of equanimity in the sense of reflective discernment.
This person brings these factors of enlightenment together upon this object.
Therefore it is said:
"He brings the factors of enlightenment together.
And he understands their domain... [and so on].
Therefore it is said:
"And he penetrates what is possible.
How does he bring the path together? How does he bring the path together?
It brings together right view in the sense of seeing; it brings together right intention in the sense of directing onto;
it brings together right speech in the sense of embracing; it brings together right action in the sense of originating;
it brings together right livelihood in the sense of cleansing; it brings together right effort in the sense of exertion; [it brings together right mindfulness] in the sense of establishing...
He brings together right mindfulness; he brings together right concentration in the sense of non-distraction.
This person brings this path together upon this object.
Therefore it is said:
“He integrates the path.
He understands the domain...
[as before] ...therefore it is said:
“And he penetrates what is possible.
How does he bring the factors of the Dhamma together?
He brings the faculties together in the sense of predominance; he brings the powers together in the sense of unshakability; [he brings them together] in the sense of outlet...
He combines the factors of enlightenment in the sense of cause; he combines the path in the sense of cause; he combines the foundations of mindfulness in the sense of establishment;
he combines the right efforts in the sense of exertion; he combines the bases of power in the sense of success;
he combines the truths in the sense of suchness; he combines serenity in the sense of non-distraction.
One unifies insight in the sense of contemplation; one unifies serenity and insight in the sense of a single flavor;
one unifies the pair [of serenity and insight] in the sense of non-excess; one unifies purification of virtue in the sense of restraint;
one unifies purification of mind in the sense of non-distraction; and one unifies purification of view in the sense of seeing.
One combines liberation in the sense of being freed; one combines clear knowledge in the sense of penetration;
one combines deliverance in the sense of relinquishment; one combines the knowledge of destruction in the sense of eradication;
one combines the knowledge of non-arising in the sense of subsiding; one combines desire in the sense of the root; and one combines attention in the sense of the origin.
He brings them together: he brings contact together in the sense of convergence; he brings feeling together in the sense of meeting;
he brings concentration together in the sense of being foremost; he brings mindfulness together in the sense of sovereignty;

he brings wisdom together in the sense of being supreme; he brings liberation together in the sense of the core; he brings Nibbāna, which plunges into the deathless, together in the sense of the ultimate goal.
This person combines these phenomena with this object.
Therefore, it is said:
“He combines phenomena.”
"He understands the sphere" means that whatever is its object is its sphere;
he understands whatever is its sphere as its object—this refers to the person.
Understanding is wisdom.
Equanimity is the evenness of the appearance of the object; equanimity is the non-distraction of the mind; equanimity is the resolution of the mind; equanimity is the purification of the mind.
"Meaning" refers to the meaning of blamelessness, the meaning of freedom from defilement, the meaning of purification, and the ultimate meaning.

"He penetrates" means he penetrates the meaning of the appearance of the object, he penetrates the meaning of the non-distraction of the mind, he penetrates the meaning of the resolution of the mind, and he penetrates the meaning of the purification of the mind.
Therefore it is said:
“And he penetrates its capacity.
How, while breathing in short, does he know: “I am breathing in short”? How, while breathing out short, does he know: “I am breathing out short”?
He breathes in a short in-breath reckoned as brief; he breathes out a short out-breath reckoned as brief; he breathes in and breathes out a short in-and-out-breath reckoned as brief.
As he breathes in and breathes out a short in-and-out-breath reckoned as brief, zeal arises.
Through the influence of that zeal, he breathes in a shorter in-breath than before, reckoned as brief.
By means of desire, he breathes out a shorter inhalation and exhalation that is subtler than before, reckoned as short.
By means of desire, he both breathes in and breathes out a shorter inhalation and exhalation that is subtler than before, reckoned as short.
While he both breathes in and breathes out a shorter inhalation and exhalation that is subtler than before, reckoned as short, by means of desire, joy arises.
By way of gladness, he breathes in a short, subtler inhalation reckoned as "limited";
by way of gladness, he breathes out a short, subtler exhalation reckoned as "limited";
by way of gladness, he breathes in and breathes out a short, subtler inhalation and exhalation reckoned as "limited."

Through the influence of gladness, as one breathes in and breathes out short inhalations and exhalations that are subtler than those [preceding], which are reckoned as short, the mind turns away from the short inhalations and exhalations, and equanimity becomes established.
In these nine ways, the short inhalations and exhalations are the body, mindfulness is the establishment, and knowledge is the contemplation.
The body is the establishment, but it is not the mindfulness.
Mindfulness is both the establishment and the mindfulness itself.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one contemplates that body;
therefore it is said:
“Development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body.
As for “contemplates”: how does one contemplate that body?
… [as detailed] … in this way one contemplates that body.
"Development" refers to the four kinds of development ... [and so on] ...
development in the sense of repeated practice.
For one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction by means of short in-breaths and out-breaths, feelings arise known ... [and so on] ...
Understanding one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of short inhalation and exhalation, he coordinates the faculties...
[as before] ...therefore it is said:
"and he penetrates what is possible."
How does one train thus: “I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body,” and how does one train thus: “I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body”?
“Body” refers to two bodies:
the mental body and the physical body.
What is the mental body (nāmakāya)?
Feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, and that which is called "name" and the "mental body," as well as those things called mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra)—
this is the mental body.
What is the form-body (rūpakāya)?
The four great elements, the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) of the four great elements, inhalation and exhalation, the sign and the focal point, and those which are called bodily formations—
this is the form-body.
How are those bodies directly known?
For one who understands the unification and non-distraction of the mind by means of long inhalation, mindfulness is established.
By that mindfulness and by that knowledge, those bodies are directly known.
For one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction by means of long out-breaths, mindfulness is established.
By that mindfulness and that knowledge, those bodies are clearly comprehended.
For one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction by means of short in-breaths, mindfulness is established.
By that mindfulness and by that knowledge, those bodies are clearly understood.
For one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction through short out-breaths, mindfulness is established.
By that mindfulness and by that knowledge, those bodies are clearly understood.
As he adverts to them, those bodies are clearly understood; as he understands them, those bodies are clearly understood; as he sees them, those bodies are clearly understood;
as he reviews them, those bodies are clearly understood; as he resolves his mind upon them, those bodies are clearly understood;
as he resolves with faith, those bodies are clearly understood; [as he exerts] energy...
Those bodies are fully understood by one who exerts himself; they are fully understood by one who establishes mindfulness;
they are fully understood by one who concentrates the mind; they are fully understood by one who understands with wisdom;
they are fully understood by one who directly knows what is to be directly known; they are fully understood by one who fully understands what is to be fully understood.
For one who abandons what is to be abandoned, those bodies are directly known; for one who develops what is to be developed, those bodies are directly known;
for one who realizes what is to be realized, those bodies are directly known.
In this way, those bodies are directly known.
Breathing in and out while experiencing the whole body is the body; mindfulness is the establishment, and knowledge is the contemplation.
The body is the establishment, but not the mindfulness.
Mindfulness is both the establishment and the mindfulness.
With that mindfulness and with that knowledge, one contemplates that body.
Therefore, it is called "the development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body in the body."
"He contemplates" means: how does he contemplate that body? ... [as before] ...
in this way he contemplates that body.
"Development" means: the four kinds of development ... [as before] ...
It is development in the sense of repeated practice.

In the case of in-breaths and out-breaths that are experienced throughout the whole body: purification of virtue occurs in the sense of restraint; purification of mind occurs in the sense of non-distraction; and purification of view occurs in the sense of seeing.
That which therein is the sense of restraint is the training in the higher virtue.
The state of non-distraction therein is the training in higher mind;
the state of seeing therein is the training in higher wisdom.
One trains by being mindful of these three trainings, one trains by knowing them, one trains by seeing them, and one trains by reviewing them.
He trains; he trains while resolving the mind; he trains while being resolved through faith;
he trains while exerting energy; he trains while establishing mindfulness; he trains while concentrating the mind; he trains while understanding with wisdom;
he trains while directly knowing what is to be directly known; he trains while fully understanding what is to be fully understood.
One trains in abandoning what is to be abandoned; one trains in developing what is to be developed; one trains in realizing what is to be realized.
For one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction through mindfulness of breathing while experiencing the whole body, feelings arise as they are known...
[and so on] ...For one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction through mindfulness of breathing while experiencing the whole body, the faculties are brought into harmony.
Therefore it is said:
"And he penetrates what is possible.
How does he train thus: "I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation," and how does he train thus: "I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation"?
What is bodily formation?
Long inhalations are bodily;
these phenomena, being bound up with the body, are bodily formations.
He trains in calming, ceasing, and pacifying those bodily formations.
Long out-breaths are bodily;
these phenomena are bound up with the body and are bodily formations.
He trains in calming, stopping, and pacifying those bodily formations.
Short inhalations and short exhalations—
exhalations and inhalations that are bodily and involve the experiencing of the whole body.
These phenomena are bound up with the body; they are bodily formations.
He trains in calming, stopping, and pacifying those bodily formations.
By means of whatever bodily formations there are that cause the bending, inclining, leaning, and bowing of the body, as well as its quivering, trembling, shaking, and agitation—
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.
By means of such bodily formations that there is no bending, no stretching, no inclining, no bowing of the body—no moving, no shaking, no wavering, no trembling—he trains thus:
"I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation, which is peaceful and subtle."
He trains thus: "Calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe out.
Thus, it seems, he trains thinking, "Calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe in," and he trains thinking, "Calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe out.

This being so, there would be no development of the perception of wind, no development of inhalation and exhalation, no development of mindfulness of breathing, and no development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing.
And wise people neither enter nor emerge from that attainment. Thus, it is said, one trains thus:
"I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation," and one trains thus: "I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.
This being so, there is the development of the perception of wind, there is the development of in-breaths and out-breaths, and there is the development of mindfulness of breathing.
And there is the development of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing;
and wise people both enter into that attainment and emerge from it.
How is this so?
Just as when a gong is struck, first coarse sounds arise;
because the sign of those coarse sounds was well apprehended, well attended to, and well retained, even when the coarse sounds have ceased, then afterwards subtle sounds arise.

Because the sign of those subtle sounds was well apprehended, well attended to, and well retained, even when the subtle sounds have ceased, then afterwards the mind still proceeds with the sign of the subtle sounds as its object.
In the same way, at first, coarse inhalations and exhalations occur.

Because the sign of the coarse inhalations and exhalations has been well apprehended, well attended to, and well retained, even when the coarse inhalations and exhalations have ceased, subsequently subtle inhalations and exhalations occur.
Because the sign of the subtle inhalations and exhalations has been well apprehended, well attended to, and well retained...
Even when the subtle inhalations and exhalations have ceased, thereafter the mind does not go to distraction even regarding the sign as the object of those subtle inhalations and exhalations.

This being so, there is the development of the perception of wind, there is the development of the inhalations and exhalations, there is the development of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*), and there is the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing.
And wise people both enter and emerge from that attainment.
Calming the bodily formation, the inhalation and exhalation are the body; mindfulness is the establishment, and knowledge is the contemplation.
The body is the establishment, but it is not the mindfulness.
Mindfulness is both the establishment [of mindfulness] and mindfulness itself.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one contemplates that body.
Therefore it is said:
“Development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body.
As for “he contemplates”: how does he contemplate that body?
… [as above] … in this way he contemplates that body.
"Development" refers to the four kinds of development ... [as above] ...
development in the sense of repetition.

While tranquilizing the bodily formation, there is purification of virtue in the sense of restraint of in-breathing and out-breathing; purification of mind in the sense of non-distraction; and purification of view in the sense of seeing.
Whatever therein is the sense of restraint, this is the training in higher virtue;
whatever therein is the sense of non-distraction, this is the training in higher mind;
whatever therein is the sense of seeing, this is the training in higher wisdom.

This is the first basis for rapture. What is the second basis for rapture? Herein, a bhikkhu, withdrawn from sensual pleasures, withdrawn from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Whatever joy there is in that rapture and happiness born of seclusion, this is called the second basis for rapture. What is the third basis for rapture? Herein, a bhikkhu, with the subsiding of thought and examination, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is internal serenity of mind, a unification of mind, free from thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of concentration. Whatever joy there is in that rapture and happiness born of concentration, this is called the third basis for rapture. What is the fourth basis for rapture? Herein, a bhikkhu, with the fading away as well of rapture, dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: "He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily.
